title: The Eighty-Word List Test
takeaway: When the model reads an 80-word list, the workspace readout holds only around six unrelated words at a time, with older entries silently dropping out. Related words behave differently: within a few items, nearly the whole category loads at once, unread members included. What clears old entries is not the passage of tokens but the arrival of a new category.
walkthrough:
The figure reports the paper's [[word-list-experiment]], a behavioral probe of how much the [[j-space]] can hold. The model reads a comma-separated list of 80 words. At every comma, the [[j-lens-readout]] is taken at each layer of the [[workspace-layers]] band. A list word counts as present if its best rank, over that band, falls within the top 25 vocabulary tokens.

Panel A shows two example readouts, taken at layer 79 under the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] convention. After one word ("shark,") the readout already contains a neighborhood of related words — "whale," "fish," "swimming," "submarine," "ocean" — almost none of which have appeared in the list. After eight animals, the readout is dominated by animal words, read or not. Highlighting marks the words actually read.

Panel B is the main count. The x-axis is the comma position; the y-axis is how many list words are present. Blue traces lists of unrelated words. The solid blue line plateaus at around six words and stays flat: entries beyond the most recent few simply drop out. Orange traces single-family lists, pooled over four families. There the dashed line, which counts all 80 list words, climbs to nearly the full family within the first few items. The paper reads this as [[category-loading]]: the workspace is not recalling many list entries but representing their shared category, using the collection of lens vectors that constitute it. Shading gives the interquartile range. Panel C varies the rank threshold $K$ and shows the qualitative picture does not depend on the choice of 25; grey control words that never appear in the prompt set the chance level.

Panels D, E, and F show [[category-displacement]]. In D, the animal list continues with color words; after a single color, the animals are largely evicted. In E, lists are built from four consecutive 20-word category blocks, with random lists in grey. Panel F plots, for each list word (row) and comma (column), the probability of appearing in the top 25: each category enters at its block's start, persists through it, and is cleared within a few words of the switch.

The figure is the paper's evidence for [[j-space-capacity]] as a functional limit, an analogue of the [[workspace-capacity-limit]] in [[working-memory]]. The count in panel B pools all workspace layers; at a single layer the number of unrelated items falls to one or two ([[single-layer-capacity]]).

terms.definition: The J-lens read operation: the residual stream at a layer is passed through the lens to produce a score for every vocabulary token, and the tokens are ranked by that score. Here it is taken at each comma of the list.

The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors — the representations the paper argues form the model's workspace. This figure measures how many words it can hold at once.
The middle band of layers where the J-space carries workspace-like content. A word's presence is judged by its best rank anywhere in this band, so panel B's counts pool over layers.
A word's position in the readout's ordering of all vocabulary tokens, taken at its best (lowest) value over the workspace layers. Rank within the top 25 counts as present.
The presence threshold: a list word is counted as in the readout if its best rank is 25 or better. Panel C shows the findings are not sensitive to this choice.
The token position at which the lens is read — one measurement after each list word, so the x-axes of panels B, D, E, and F advance one comma per word.
The layer of panel A's example readouts. The paper indexes 25 evenly spaced layers as 0-100, so 79 reads as roughly 79% of the model's depth — late in the workspace band.
Example layer-79 readouts after one word and after eight words of an animal list, with the words actually read highlighted. It shows related but unread words entering the readout immediately.
The first word of panel A's example list. After it alone, the readout already contains "whale," "fish," "swimming," "submarine," and "ocean," almost none of which have appeared in the list.
The main count: number of list words present in the readout at each comma, for single-family lists (orange) versus unrelated lists (blue).
80-word lists drawn from one category, such as animals. Results are pooled over four families. These load the readout as a whole category within a few items.
80-word lists of items with no shared category, drawn at random. Only around six of the words read so far are present at any comma, and the count stays flat.
In panels B, D, and E: the count restricted to words the model has already read.
In panel B: the count over all 80 list words, unread ones included. For single-family lists it rises to nearly the full family within the first few items — the signature of category loading.
The band around each curve, spanning the 25th to 75th percentile over trials.
A robustness check: the number of already-read words at rank K or better, measured near the end of the list, as the threshold K varies. It shows the top-25 cutoff is not doing the work.
The rank cutoff varied along panel C's x-axis; the rest of the figure fixes it at 25.
Words that never appear in the prompt, counted the same way. They set the chance level against which the list words' presence is judged.
The animal list of panel A continued with color words. After even one color word, the readout is dominated by colors and the animals are largely evicted.
Counts for blocked lists: four consecutive 20-word blocks, each of one category. Each category enters at its block's start, persists through it, and is cleared within a few words of the switch.
Unstructured lists plotted alongside the blocked ones for comparison; they show the flat roughly-six-word plateau rather than block structure.

A heatmap over the blocked lists: for each list word (row) and each comma (column), the probability of that word appearing in the top-25 readout. The block structure appears as four diagonal bands that cut off at each category switch.
Example word categories used in panels A and D; two of the categories from which the single-family and blocked lists are built.

numbers.meaning: Words per list. Long enough to far exceed the roughly six-word plateau for unrelated words, so displacement is visible, and to make full-family loading (the dashed orange line approaching 80) unmistakable.
The rank threshold for counting a word as present in the readout. Panel C varies this cutoff and finds the qualitative findings do not depend on it.

How many already-read unrelated words are present at any given comma. The count stays flat as the list continues — words beyond the most recent few drop out. This is the figure's functional capacity estimate for unrelated content, pooled over the workspace layers.

The same count at a single workspace layer (layer 79, shown in an appendix figure the text cites). Presence anywhere in the band is a lenient criterion; per layer, capacity for unrelated items is smaller still.
Two uses: the number of word families pooled into panel B's orange curves, and the number of consecutive category blocks in panel E's lists.
Words per category block in the panel E and F lists; four blocks of 20 make up the 80.
The layer of panel A's example readouts, in the paper's 0-100 percentage indexing — a late workspace layer, roughly 79% of the model's depth.
The two snapshots in panel A: the readout after a single list word and after eight. One word already pulls in a neighborhood of related words; eight lock the readout onto the shared category.

Panel D's list: eight animals followed by eight color words. A single color word suffices to displace the animal representations, showing eviction is driven by the category switch rather than by list length.
